score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: This design handles the scenario fairly well because immutable audit anchors, append-only local records, and supersession references help preserve history when Carol asks to mutate something after freeze. It strongly supports audit and later reconstruction of what changed. However, it does not define explicit freeze lineage rules, so the key scenario decision—new specimen, superseding pCID, or amendment—remains under-specified. It is also more claim-card-centric than promise-first in vocabulary.
strengths: Exact immutable audit anchors preserve pre-freeze evidence and make history hard to rewrite.
Local append-only promise-accounting records fit peer-local audit and sparse knowledge.
Plane separation helps avoid conflating live behavior, durable audit publication, storage, and device effects.
Supersedes/rotation references provide a plausible path for post-freeze evolution without mutating old evidence.
weaknesses: Freeze semantics are implicit rather than first-class in the simulation.
The design does not fully specify how lineage decisions are made for breaking post-freeze changes.
Promise vocabulary is diluted by claim-card and conformance-style framing.
The combined card-plus-anchor-plus-record pattern is more complex than the smallest durable artifact set.
risks: Teams may treat scoped claim cards as normative conformance badges instead of local promises plus evidence.
Without an explicit freeze/supersession rule, different peers may classify the same post-freeze change differently.
The artifact set can grow into a heavier wrapper than needed for very small durable deployments.
open_questions: What exact rule decides whether a post-freeze mutation becomes a new specimen, a superseding pCID, or a lineage amendment?
How should freeze evidence be represented explicitly in the claim-card/audit-anchor pattern?
Who is allowed to publish superseding lineage claims without making promises on behalf of other peers?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Peers publish their own scoped cards and keep their own append-only promise-accounting records; no central actor is required.

scoped_intent.note: Scope is explicit by plane and status, but the primary artifact is still a claim card rather than a direct promise-form declaration of intent.

no_promises_for_others.note: Scoped cards are meant to be published by the relevant embodiment or service, though shared-family linkage needs care not to over-speak for sibling agents.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: The design records attempts, receipts, failures, and break-witnesses instead of guaranteeing retention, delivery, or physical effect completion.

local_trust_assessment.note: Local audit anchors and append-only records support peer-local trust assessment, but 'authoritative boundary identity' language risks sounding more global than local.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: The design separates hash/address possession, authorization, retention, and retrieval promises rather than treating receipt or use as obligation.

violations: Primary framing uses claim/conformance artifacts more than explicit promise-first declarations.
'Authoritative boundary identity' wording can drift toward non-local authority semantics unless carefully reframed.
